extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, and practitioners interested in U.S. First Amendment exceptions
extracted.subtask_description: A survey of categories of speech that receive lesser or no protection under the U.S. First Amendment and the legal tests/standards and special-government-capacity exceptions the courts apply. The page summarizes doctrinal rules (tests, balancing frameworks) and leading cases illustrating each exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement (imminent lawless action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has held that "advocacy of the use of force" is unprotected when it is "directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action" and is "likely to incite or produce such action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evolution from the earlier "clear and present danger" test (Schenck) to Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) which narrowed liability to advocacy that is directed to and likely to produce imminent lawless action; distinguishes protected 'mere advocacy' from punishable incitement. Cases cited: Schenck v. United States; Brandenburg v. Ohio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement to suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly encouraging someone to commit suicide can be unprotected speech and lead to criminal liability (example: involuntary manslaughter conviction in Massachusetts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses a Massachusetts juvenile-court and state-high-court prosecution (Michelle Carter texting case), later left in place when U.S. Supreme Court declined review; shows that courts may treat persistent encouragement of self-harm as criminal depending on intent and causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no constitutional value in false statements of fact' (Gertz), but the Court uses a complex framework to determine which false statements are unprotected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four explicit areas: (1) knowingly making false statements of fact can sometimes be punished (e.g., libel where requisite state of mind shown); (2) negligently false statements may lead to civil liability in some instances; (3) some implicit statements of fact (with a 'false factual connotation') can be exception-worthy; (4) some false statements (notably certain lies about the government) may be fully protected per New York Times v. Sullivan. Also notes perjury and materiality issues, and case law like United States v. Alvarez (Stolen Valor) and Riley v. NF of the Blind (telemarketing/charitable solicitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech (diminished protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech does not enjoy full First Amendment protection; it receives 'diminished protection' and may be regulated more readily than political speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False or misleading advertising can be punished; restrictions on advertising are permissible if they advance a substantial governmental interest and are not overly broad (Central Hudson balancing principle). Examples include telemarketing anti-fraud laws and false advertising cases. The doctrine rests on a policy balancing that political speech is more important than commercial speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech owned by others (intellectual property exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible restrictions on speech can be based on intellectual property rights; copyrights and trade secrets fall under this exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has upheld IP-based limits (e.g., Harper & Row v. Nation Enterprises) and recognizes broadcasting/airtime allocation as a property-like restriction; rationale includes protecting incentives in the 'speech marketplace.' Also notes trade secrets and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeit currency and reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws against counterfeit U.S. currency and some realistic reproductions have been consistently upheld as outside First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress's power to punish counterfeiting (Art. I, §8) supports regulation; cases and examples include prosecutions or restrictions on realistic currency art and depictions when they could be feasibly passed off as real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting words
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech is unprotected if it constitutes 'fighting words'—words that 'tend[s] to incite an immediate breach of the peace' by provoking a fight and are personally abusive when addressed to the ordinary citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined in Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942). Additional requirements: speech must be directed to the person of the hearer and be likely understood as a direct personal insult. The doctrine is narrow; courts have limited and refined it through later cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: True threats
rubrics_metrics.description: 'True threats of violence' directed at a person or group with intent of placing the target at risk of bodily harm or death are generally unprotected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider intent and how a reasonable person would perceive the statement; some hyperbole is protected (if a reasonable person would view it as obvious hyperbole). Threats of social ostracism or politically motivated boycotts have been found protected. Relevant cases: Virginia v. Black; Watts v. United States; Elonis/Counterman contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threatening the president (statutory special rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 18 U.S.C. §871 it is illegal to knowingly and willfully make any threat to take the life of, kidnap, or inflict bodily harm upon the President (and certain successors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from general true-threat law because the statute does not require the threatener to have the capability to carry out the threat (e.g., prisoners can be charged). Courts have upheld convictions under this statutory provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech integral to criminal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that is integral to illegal conduct can be restricted; speech that facilitates or is part of committing a crime is not protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references speech related to criminal conduct (e.g., New York v. Ferber on child sexual exploitation, United States v. Hansen on fraudulent immigration-related speech). Such speech is treated differently because it's inseparable from the underlying criminal activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity (Miller test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Miller test, speech is unprotected as obscene if: (1) the average person, applying contemporary community standards, would find that the work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest; (2) the work depicts or describes sexual conduct in a patently offensive way as defined by state law; and (3) the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'prurient interest' = shameful or morbid interest in sex, and that a person may only be punished if he knows the contents; some private possession limitations exist. Cases cited include Miller v. California and subsequent obscenity decisions. The rationale includes perceived corrupting/debasing social impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child pornography exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Child pornography is unprotected even beyond the Miller framework: visual depictions of minors engaged in sexual acts or lewd exhibitions of genitals are categorically unprotected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception is more concrete: if material visually depicts minors in sexual contexts it is unprotected and private possession may be outlawed (New York v. Ferber, Osborne v. Ohio). It does not depend on Miller's prurient/value balancing and does not apply to adult pornography merely thought harmful to children.

rubrics_metrics.name: As employer (public employee speech rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government generally cannot fire an employee for speech if three criteria are met: the speech addresses a matter of public concern; the speech is not made pursuant to the employee's job duties but as a citizen; and the damage inflicted on the government by the speech does not outweigh the value of the speech to the employee and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the Garcetti/Connick/Pickering framework: determine public-concern status (content, form, context), then balance the government's interest in an efficient workplace against the employee's speech value (Pickering balancing). Cases cited: GARCETTI v. Ceballos; Connick v. Myers; Pickering v. Board of Education.

rubrics_metrics.name: As regulator of the communications industry (broadcasting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of speech on broadcast radio and television is permissible when narrowly tailored and furthering a substantial governmental interest (e.g., shielding listeners/children from offensive ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court has confined such rules to traditional broadcasting and refused to extend them broadly to the internet. Cases include Red Lion, FCC v. Pacifica, and refusal in other contexts such as efforts to regulate internet content. Emphasis on narrow tailoring and substantial interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: News and privacy / Right to a fair trial (gag orders, prior restraint considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may impose certain constraints to protect fair trials and privacy interests, but these areas involve complex balancing against First Amendment protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes gaps and cross-references prior restraint, gag orders, and landmark cases (Estes, Sheppard, Neb. Press Ass'n v. Stuart). Sections flagged as needing expansion; the rubric is that restrictions must be justified against free-press/free-speech rights and not be an improper prior restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: As educator (student speech in K–12)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government acts as a K–12 educator, it may restrict student speech when that speech 'materially and substantially interferes with the requirements of appropriate discipline in the operation of the school.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Tinker v. Des Moines (1969); later cases added exceptions allowing restriction of student speech about drugs, 'vulgar and offensive' language, and school-run newspapers (e.g., Bethel, Hazelwood, Morse). Basis: in loco parentis giving schools broader discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: As subsidizer or speaker (government speech and funding conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government can express its own message and favor viewpoints when speaking as government, but when subsidizing private speech it must generally act viewpoint-neutrally if it is providing a forum for diverse private views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subsidy programs are 'indiscriminate' they must be viewpoint-neutral (Legal Services Corp. v. Velazquez); the government cannot impose conditions on how subsidy recipients spend money they obtain from other sources. Distinguishes government speech (broad leeway) from regulation of funded private speech (scrutinized for viewpoint discrimination).

rubrics_metrics.name: As regulator of the bar and legal proceedings (attorney speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has greater power to regulate the speech of lawyers, using a balancing test weighing the State's legitimate interest in regulation against the interests of the attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While attorney advertising is generally protected to some degree, rules of professional conduct and ethical guidelines are permissible; examples and cases include Ohralik, Gentile, and other attorney-regulation jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: As controller/operator of the military
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government has extremely broad power to restrict the speech of military officers and personnel, beyond what would be permitted for civilians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parker v. Levy (1974) affirmed the military's status as a specialized society needing stricter speech limits. The article notes limited subsequent case law developing specific limits; deference to military necessity is a guiding principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: As prison warden (inmate speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government controls prisons it may limit inmate speech so long as restrictions are 'reasonably related to legitimate penological interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard (Turner/Turner-like analyses) applies broadly to inmates, pretrial detainees, and many on probation/parole. The only recognized limit in the article is the requirement to provide an 'alternate means of exercising that right' so that legitimate speech can still be expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: As regulator of immigration (noncitizen speech at borders/immigration consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may not criminally punish immigrants based on speech that would be protected for citizens, but on entry it may bar non-citizens from the United States based on their speech; rules regarding deportation for speech are less clear and are split among lower courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that border-entry decisions allow broader exclusion based on speech; deportation standards are unsettled and courts are divided, with leading cases dating to Red Scare-era jurisprudence. Recent cases (e.g., Hansen) may inform the modern approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate speech is not a general First Amendment exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech, by itself, is not a general exception to First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites multiple sources and Supreme Court reaffirmations that there is no standalone 'hate speech' exception; hate-crime enhancements (Wisconsin v. Mitchell) are permissible because they punish conduct or use speech as evidence of motive rather than criminalizing the speech alone.
